title: CDI Listening Test 25
description: A full Listening test from the CDI practice materials, with the original recording. 4 parts, 40 questions.

parts.transcript:
You will hear a telephone conversation between a man who is finding out about a preschool for his young daughter and a woman who works there.
Sally: Good morning, Riverdale Preschool, Sally speaking.
Robert: Hello, my name’s Robert. I’ve got a four-year-old daughter called Susie, and I’d like to get some information about your preschool, please.
Sally: Sure, Robert. Well, Susie’s the right age. We take three and four-year-olds in classes of 20 students.
Robert: Oh great. And how many teachers do you have?
Sally: We have two. The first group is taught by Mrs. Oliver, and the second group is taken by Mrs. Keogh.
Robert: Just a moment, I’ll write that down. Could you spell the last name please?
Sally: Yes, it’s K-E-O-G-H.
Robert: Okay. Now, I know the children attend for two or three days a week.
Sally: That’s right. The older ones, like Susie, are here for three days, which means 15 hours a week. The younger ones, the three-year-olds, attend two days a week — 10 hours.
Robert: And what do they do during that time?
Sally: Well, half the day is spent outside — running, playing, or a calmer activity like painting. We have a great outside play area that we’re improving all the time.
Robert: You’ve recently put in a new slide, haven’t you?
Sally: Yes, we’re really pleased with it. The children love it.
Robert: And are you thinking of adding anything else outdoors?
Sally: We were hoping to build a playhouse, but that was too expensive. So we’re now making plans for a garden where the children will be able to grow flowers and vegetables.
Sally: The other half of the day is spent indoors. This year the children seem to be very interested in music, so the teachers are doing a lot of activities related to that. Last year, there was more interest in dancing.
Sally: The teachers may sometimes play quiet games, but we always make time for a story each day. It’s a very important part of the program here.
Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.
Robert: Now, I’d like to ask about the fees.
Sally: Sure. We actually had to put them up this term.
Robert: I heard it used to be $420 but it’s just gone up to $470. Is that right?
Sally: Yes. We had to add the extra $50 to cover costs.
Robert: My friend also told me about a trip to the local zoo.
Sally: Yes, we did that last year, but we’ll be going to a farm this year instead.
Sally: Also included in the price is membership of a special library. Children can borrow a toy and keep it for a week.
Sally: The children have a rest here during the day, and we make up a little bed. But we advise parents to pack a pillow in the child’s bag, as we don’t provide one.
Robert: What if I want to come and look around?
Sally: The best thing is to call the teacher on the classroom mobile. The number is 0914 638 520.

parts.transcript:
You will hear part of a talk about how students can get help finding a part-time job while they’re studying.
Marissa: Hi, thanks for coming along. My name’s Marissa, and I’m going to tell you a bit about finding part-time jobs. Not everybody wants to work when they’re studying, but you may need to earn some extra cash. However, if you are a student from overseas, there may be particular conditions attached to working in this country.
Marissa: The university has its own job centre on the campus. Well actually, it’s not on this main Hillston campus, it’s based in the student services building on the campus called Woodside. Spelt W-O-O-D-S-I-D-E. The centre works on a drop-in basis. It’s open six days a week, Monday to Saturday, nine hours a day, from ten in the morning until eight at night.
Marissa: The centre is run by other students, but a professional employment lawyer is on hand every Tuesday if you want any advice.
Marissa: Part-time jobs become available almost every day, and they are advertised on the university website, which you can access through the library if the computer centre is closed.
Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.
Marissa: They’re looking for people to check that all the vehicles using the university car parks have got up-to-date permits. Office jobs rarely come up, but in future the university is hoping to offer jobs in the IT centre.
Marissa: There are also recruitment open days, held regularly during the year, when local employers come into the university to recruit students.
Marissa: Part-time work is also a valuable way of building up an employment record that reflects your skills and capabilities.
Marissa: Students who work part-time can no longer expect to be paid cash. An employer will deduct tax from what you earn.
Marissa: Make sure your employer knows in good time if you’re ill. That shouldn’t be a problem now that everyone has a mobile phone. And if you decide to leave the job, make sure you put this in writing.

parts.transcript:
You will hear a sociology student called John discussing his research project about the use of public services with his tutor.
Tutor: Hello John. You’re here to discuss your research project, are you?
John: Yes. I want to look at how people use public services in their local area.
Tutor: Do you have a special interest in public services?
John: Not really. It’s just that I found a report in the college library about an investigation done 10 years ago, and I thought it’d be interesting to do a parallel one.
John: I think there’ll be some differences. For example, the number of people going to the library will have decreased. And I’d guess that older people are using the sports centre more often than they used to.
Tutor: Now, what sort of data are you going to use?
John: Official records from the local council. They should be easy to obtain.
Tutor: There might not be as much information as you’d like, but it’d certainly be the easiest kind of data to work with. Have you considered using a questionnaire as well?
Tutor: You’ve already done the module on questionnaire design. And it’ll be good to get experience, because next year you’ll have to do something similar for your final dissertation.
Tutor: Are you going to look at people’s level of education? Whether they have a degree?
John: I hadn’t planned to.
Tutor: Well, you might see some interesting patterns.
John: Okay. And that’ll tie in nicely with my plans to analyse the kind of work people do. — adding qualifications.
John: I don’t think I can analyse more than 50, so I should probably distribute about 80 questionnaires altogether, to allow for wastage.
Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.
Tutor: To make sure that your questions make sense, you should try them out beforehand.
John: My friends will help.
John: I could enclose a stamped envelope for the return post. It’s a bit expensive, but I think it’d be worth it.
John: Would it be a good idea to have a short paragraph at the top explaining what I’m doing and why?
Tutor: Definitely. And don’t forget, you’ll need to get a bit of information about your subjects. What age group they’re in and how long they’ve lived in the area.
Tutor: In this case, I’d stick to closed questions. The results will be much more manageable.

parts.transcript:
You will hear a tutor talking to a group of students about a project to build a driverless vehicle.
Tutor: The university has decided to enter an international competition next year. The engineering school will be collaborating with the computer science department, and possibly the automotive design department.
Tutor: The vehicles must cover the whole distance without a human driver, and avoid unexpected hazards. Things like rocks, for example.
Tutor: There was one design which we will be analysing carefully. That particular vehicle built a three-dimensional picture of its surroundings using video cameras and lasers. It was equipped with seven laptop computers.
Tutor: The sponsors are hoping to see innovative design ideas that they can transfer into commercial production — to find useful new design features.
Tutor: Programming skills will decide who eventually wins first prize — success depends on the software design.
Tutor: Even after months of planning, many teams were amazed that the vehicles did what they wanted them to do at all — surprised they were as successful as they were.
Tutor: At the beginning of May, we’ll be scheduling a seminar to introduce the project. Later in May, we’ll be asking you to submit a short essay telling us about any particular skills that you have.
Tutor: In June, we’re organising a trip to a factory. Then in September, we’ll hold a weekend workshop to share ideas and see computer-aided design demonstrations.
Tutor: In December, submit your outline designs, and the following month we’ll choose the team and start work in earnest.
